transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-11-05
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes (approx)
Language: English
Attendees: Maya Patel, Ethan Ruiz (Redwood); Janelle Cho, Ravi Menon, Liam O'Neill (VectorStream)

Summary:
Quick intro between partnership/alliances teams; primary focus is on technical onramp for VectorStream's managed edge cloud customers. Main discussion points: hosted vs dedicated onramp, VPC/private control plane requirements, GPU types and quantization support, routing/fallback, security/compliance (SOC2/KMS), pilot success criteria and next steps.

Topics:
- Partner program alignment and commercial model (brief)
- Private/on-prem onramp integration patterns
- Inference runtime compatibility and GPU SKUs
- Observability and billing signals
- Pilot scope and timeline

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um this is Maya from Redwood, with Ethan on the line too. How are you folks doing?
[00:05] Janelle: Good thanks, yeah happy to be here. We, uh, we're excited to see how Redwood could help with our onramp work.
[00:12] Ravi: Hi, Ravi here. Quick note, we'll be joined by Liam who manages the infra side — hi Liam.
[00:16] Liam: Hey all.
[00:20] Maya: Awesome. Quick round — Maya's AE, Ethan's our SE, he'll handle the deep infra bits. Janelle, do you want to kick off with what VectorStream is trying to accomplish?
[00:28] Janelle: Sure. So VectorStream we run a managed edge cloud for telco and retail verticals. We're looking to offer a simple LLM onramp to our customers - something they can turn on as a managed feature. The ask is: low-friction integration, predictable latency SLAs, and controls for data residency. We're evaluating partners for both hosted model access and an option to onboard onto our private clusters.
[00:48] Maya: Got it. Are you thinking of Redwood hosted API or a private deployment — or both?
[00:53] Janelle: Both. Start with hosted for quick time-to-market but need a clear path to private/VPC for enterprise customers.
[00:59] Ethan: Makes sense. From a technical lens there's two typical patterns we see: 1) quick hosted integration where your users call the Redwood API and we route to hosted models, 2) private onramp where we deploy a customer-specific control plane inside your VPC or on-prem and either run inference in your infra or in a dedicated pool. Each has tradeoffs on latency, cost, and operational ownership.
[01:20] Ravi: For our customers, latency to the edge is key — many are in APAC/EMEA with specific routing. Also, some customers will require KMS integration for keys and SOC2 audit trails.
[01:31] Maya: Totally, we support KMS/HSM integrations and can surface audit logs. Ethan, do you want to talk about VPC/private deployment options?
[01:37] Ethan: Yeah. For private, we offer two patterns — VPC-hosted control plane where Redwood manages the control plane but it lives in your VPC, and air-gapped on-prem packages where you manage everything. In the VPC pattern, we still run inference in either your GPU pool or in a dedicated Redwood-dedicated capacity attached to that control plane. There are nuances around KV cache, network egress, and kernel selection for different GPU SKUs.
[02:03] Liam: When you say "dedicated capacity", is that isolated GPUs or multitenant with soft isolation? What does isolation mean for our compliance teams?
[02:12] Ethan: Dedicated means physically reserved GPU pools for the customer, not multi-tenant on the same GPU card. We can provide attestations for isolation and support customer-managed keys for model artifacts. For compliance, we can also provide audit logs and longer retention as an add-on.
[02:28] Ravi: Okay good. What GPU types are compatible? We run a mix of A100s and newer H100s, and some partners have lower-power Ampere edge cards.
[02:37] Ethan: We support a broad set — A100, H100, and optimized paths for lower-memory Ampere edge SKUs. That said, model quantization and kernel selection vary. For example, some 4-bit quant profiles work well on Ampere edge with our quant runtime, but you lose a bit of throughput vs H100 for large context lengths.
[02:56] Janelle: Could you elaborate on quantization — we have customers who are cost-sensitive and want the cheaper cards.
[03:02] Ethan: Sure — we have tested int4 and int8 paths. With int4 you get big memory savings and lower cost, but depending on model and prompt distribution there can be small changes in output fidelity. Our Optimize tooling can recommend quant profiles per workload; for an edge onramp we'd usually run an eval on a small prompt suite to pick the sweet spot.
[03:23] Liam: What about KV cache — how do you handle cold starts for chat workloads? We need to maintain low tail latency.
[03:29] Ethan: We use prefix and KV caching per customer. In private deployments the KV cache can be colocated with the serving nodes to minimize network latency; in hosted setups we do a regional cache and automatic prefetch for expected patterns. We can also pin warm sessions for high-value customers.
[03:47] Ravi: Sounds promising. On networking, how much egress will there be? If we host control plane in VPC, will model weights be pulled across the internet?
[03:56] Maya: Good question. For VPC-hosted control plane, weights and images are pulled over secure channels and can be stored in your private registry - we can support private S3 or registry mirrors to avoid internet egress where needed.
[04:08] Janelle: I want to flag that some of our telco customers mandate that model logs cannot leave country bound—data residency.
[04:14] Ethan: We can configure regional routing policies so inference runs in region and we can redact or keep logs local. There's some config work for compliance but it's possible.
[04:24] Liam: On the latency front — any published numbers for cold vs warm? We particularly want P95 under 120ms for short completion models.
[04:32] Ethan: Our benchmarks vary by model; for smaller decoder-only models on H100 in a dedicated pool, warm P95 sub-50ms for <256 tokens is achievable. Cold starts depend on KV size and the warm state. We'll share a concise benchmark matrix after the call — that's one of the next steps.
[04:49] Ravi: Can we run our own micro-benchmarks? We want to replicate our edge patterns.
[04:53] Maya: Absolutely, we can provide a benchmarking checklist and Dockerized client or you can run our sample harness against a pilot endpoint. Ethan will coordinate.
[04:59] Ethan: I'll put together the checklist — CPU/GPU telemetry we need, typical prompt distribution, QPS, concurrency targets.
[05:06] Janelle: Commercially, what does pilot pricing look like? We may want to test with a small set of customers — 2-3 tenants.
[05:12] Maya: We usually do time-limited pilots with usage credits and a priced path to Dedicated. For partners we also have co-sell credits; I'll share a banded example in the one-pager.
[05:21] Liam: One operational thing — orchestration of model rollouts. We run canaries for new models. Can Redwood integrate to our CI for model promotions?
[05:28] Ethan: Yes — we support CI hooks and webhook triggers for rollouts, plus canary/A B rollouts. Our console exposes model versioning and automatic fallback policies if latency or quality regress.
[05:40] Ravi: Security — we need SSO with SAML and RBAC scoped to teams. Also we need to see the map of who's accessing what.
[05:48] Maya: We support SAML SSO, SCIM for provisioning, and role-based access controls. Audit logs include token-level details if needed.
[05:55] Janelle: Are there any pitfalls with private on-prem installs we should be aware of?
[05:59] Ethan: Common ones: network bandwidth for model pulls, GPU driver mismatches, and image compatibility. We provide a compatibility matrix and a preflight script to catch env issues. Also quant kernels may need a small kernel build for certain edge cards.
[06:17] Liam: What's the typical time-to-deploy for a VPC control plane?
[06:21] Ethan: If your infra is ready and you provide IAM roles and a peering/VPN, typical is 2-4 weeks for a VPC-hosted control plane and config; on-prem air-gapped installs take longer because they need onsite validation.
[06:33] Janelle: For pilot success criteria, I'll say 1) stable integration with our billing + SSO, 2) P95 latency within agreed bounds, 3) no data leaving country for the pilot tenants, and 4) run rate cost within X of our target.
[06:48] Maya: Those are reasonable. We'll propose a pilot scope that addresses each.
[06:52] Liam: About billing signals — we need token-level or inference-level metrics to reconcile invoices.
[06:57] Maya: Our console exposes token breakdowns, cost per request, and per-model usage. We can also push usage events to your billing system via a webhook.
[07:07] Ravi: Any red flags on our side — we use a mix of Kubernetes clusters across on-prem and cloud. Will Redwood support hybrid sets?
[07:15] Ethan: Yes, hybrid is a common pattern — part of inference fleet in your edge clusters and fallback to Redwood Dedicated in our cloud, with smart routing. The key is consistent model versions and cache coherence.
[07:28] Janelle: Do you have an existing channel partner flow — revenue share or referral?
[07:33] Maya: We have a partner program with referral fees and co-sell motions; specifics we can sync on after this call with partnership ops.
[07:41] Liam: Let's talk about observability — what telemetry do we get? Traces, spans, latency histograms?
[07:46] Ethan: We export traces and span context, per-token timing, and per-request logs to your observability backend — Datadog/Prometheus/ELK. We also provide per-route dashboards and alert hooks for SLO breaches.
[07:59] Ravi: For the pilot we'll want the logs to be available in our Splunk instance and to have a retention policy that meets telco regs.
[08:06] Maya: We'll note that.
[08:09] [08:09] (brief mute/hold music)
[08:22] Janelle: A couple more questions — on model governance, how do you handle supervised model updates? We need the ability to pin a model version for a tenant.
[08:31] Ethan: You can pin per-tenant model versions, freeze updates, and apply canaries to subsets. We also support model evaluation hooks so you can run smoke tests on new versions before promotion.
[08:44] Liam: Regarding model artifacts — can we bring our own models into Redwood's serving runtime? Some of our enterprise customers want to serve custom models.
[08:52] Ethan: Yes, customers can bring models. We have onboarding for proprietary models — they can be uploaded to private registries and we support popular frameworks and a standard container spec. We do a quick compatibility check and sometimes a small instrumented run to validate performance.
[09:05] Ravi: If we bring models, what about licensing and model privacy?
[09:09] Maya: We sign NDAs and can segregate artifacts. For private deployments the model never leaves your infrastructure unless you opt-in.
[09:17] Janelle: For the pilot timeline — we'd like to target a narrow pilot window in Dec scope, deploy in early Jan with two customers. Is that realistic?
[09:24] Ethan: It's tight but doable if we start the preflight now and exchange infra artifacts.
[09:28] Maya: We'll aim for the checklist this week so you can start preflight.
[09:32] Liam: On the telemetry side, do you collect per-token embeddings? Some customers use embeddings for reranking and want to push embeddings to their vector DB in-region.
[09:40] Ethan: We can stream embeddings out and provide direct webhooks or S3 mirrors. For PII-sensitive embeddings we support in-region storage and retention policies.
[09:50] Ravi: Any experience with telco-grade throughput — millions of calls per day?
[09:54] Ethan: We have customers at that scale. The common approach is multi-tenant routing + dedicated pools per high-volume tenant and dynamic batching. We can also co-locate caches near edge points of presence.
[10:06] Janelle: How do you handle cost transparency for our customers — they will ask about per-call costs.
[10:11] Maya: Our console provides token-level costing and cost breakdowns by model and route. We can provide a per-tenant export to help reconcile.
[10:20] Liam: One last technical nit — kernel support for smaller card vendors. We saw a note about needing a kernel build; is that something you handle or we have to build?
[10:28] Ethan: We typically provide a prebuilt kernel for common edge SKUs, but for very niche cards we might need a packaged build. We'll include that in the preflight matrix.
[10:36] Janelle: Great. Maybe now we can go rapid-fire on any blockers and then recap?
[10:41] Maya: Sure. Blockers I note: security docs to review (SOC2/ISO), pilot pricing alignment, infra preflight and SSO/SAML. Anything else?
[10:51] Ravi: Also need confirmation of model artifacts lifecycle — who deletes what and retention policies.
[10:56] Ethan: We'll share the data retention and artifact lifecycle doc.
[11:00] Liam: From our side, confirm we can provide a private ECR and S3 mirror for images and artifacts.
[11:06] Maya: Yes.
[11:08] Janelle: Awesome. Recap and next steps?
[11:11] Maya: Recap: Redwood to send integration one-pager, security deck, and benchmarking checklist. VectorStream to share infra diagram, SSO requirements, and sample QPS numbers. Plan a technical deep dive week of 2025-11-17 to nail private deployment details.
[11:26] Janelle: That works.
[11:28] Ravi: We'll aim to get the diagram and numbers by 2025-11-10.
[11:31] Maya: Perfect. Anything else?
[11:33] Liam: No, thank you.
[11:36] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up.
[11:38] (call ends)

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-IDs and minor ASR substitutions (e.g., "KV cache" as "K V cash", "Dedicated" as "dedicate"), some overlapping talk not fully captured.
